en: The Śatasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra: The Samādhi of the Factors of Enlightenment,
spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai during the Sui Dynasty,
recorded by his disciple Guanding.
1. Discerning the Characteristics of Dharmas (Dharmalakṣaṇavibhaṅga), Part One.
Now, a practitioner who wishes to cross the great ocean of birth and death and ascend to the other shore of nirvāṇa must thoroughly comprehend the root of deluded afflictions.
He thoroughly knows the supreme path that leads to liberation and the root of delusive confusion;
this is precisely the ultimate reality of the mind.
The essential path to the ultimate Way is what is called reflecting back upon the source of the mind;
realizing its actual reality is precisely the true cause of Buddha-nature.
Reflecting back upon the source of the mind is the "enlightening cause" (liao-yin).
These two causes encompass all phenomena exhaustively, leaving nothing out.
For example, within the pure and clear sky,
the full orb of the sun shines with serene radiance;
yet as for this sky and this sun, [they are distinct].
Neither identical nor separate, neither abiding nor non-abiding,
it is called the excellent condition for destroying darkness and the essential method for revealing emptiness.
Although darkness is extinguished and emptiness is revealed,
emptiness itself neither diminishes nor benefits;
in truth, there is no diminution when one investigates the matter through principle.
Darkness and obscurations are forever eliminated;
its nature neither increases nor diminishes.
All myriad phenomena contained within the realm of space appear therein.
Although this nature of space is pure,
if there is no sunlight, darkness arises;
it is not that the emptiness of space can dispel the darkness by itself.
If darkness is to be dispelled,
it must rely on the light of the sun;
yet if there were no empty space, the sun could not exist.
Without light there is no illumination;
as when the sky is without the sun,
darkness cannot dispel itself.
However, this nature of darkness neither comes nor goes,
and the essence and characteristics of the sun likewise neither arise nor perish;
it is simply that the sun shines upon the sky.
Thus, when heaven and earth are thoroughly understood,
the sun of wisdom illuminates the emptiness of the mind-nature;
it is also like this.
Just as the sun is not identical to space,
yet it is not separate from space;
if the sun were identical to space, how could space illuminate?
If the sun were separated from space,
it could not rely upon space to manifest its illumination.
The sun of wisdom is likewise.
It is not that the nature of mind is empty;
it is not that apart from the nature of mind there is emptiness.
If the nature of mind were itself emptiness, [then...]
Thus, illumination does not arise because of cultivation;
yet, if one were to depart from the emptiness of the nature of mind, cultivation likewise could not produce illumination.
It is like the sun: it neither dwells in space, nor does it not dwell in space.
Because it does not abide in emptiness, it is able to illumine all that is empty;
yet because it does not fail to abide in emptiness, it ultimately does not fall into emptiness.
The sun of wisdom is also like this.
One deeply contemplates that the nature of the mind is empty, yet does not dwell in the emptiness of the nature of the mind;
it is able to illumine all things as empty because it does not fail to abide in emptiness.
Although it illumines all things, the wisdom-mind remains unmoved and does not retreat;
like the sun, it can dispel darkness and reveal the characteristics of space.
The sun of wisdom is likewise:
it can shatter the darkness of ignorance and reveal the true nature of the mind.
Just as when the sun sets, darkness appears in the sky,
yet space itself neither benefits nor suffers from it;
so too is the sun of wisdom.
It can eliminate the darkness of ignorance and reveal the true mark of the mind's essence;
yet, regarding the emptiness of the nature of mind, it neither increases nor decreases,
just as the sun does not diminish the sky.
Furthermore, it does not benefit emptiness itself;
rather, it can dispel the darkness within emptiness and reveal the myriad phenomena of the realm of space.
The sun of wisdom is also like this.
Although the nature of the mind is empty, it is neither diminished nor enhanced; yet it can sever all afflictions, accomplish the myriad practices, and manifest all phenomena.
It is like space, which, though pure, gives rise to darkness because the sun is absent.
The nature of the mind is also like this:
although it is fundamentally pure,
delusive confusion arises when the light of wisdom is absent.
Just as space, though pure, cannot remove darkness by itself,
yet the removal of darkness necessarily depends upon sunlight;
so too it is with the emptiness of the nature of mind.
Although the original nature is inherently pure, it cannot eliminate delusions by itself;
yet, for delusions to be extinguished, they must necessarily be illuminated by wisdom.
It is like the sun: if there were no space, there would be no light.
Nor is there illumination.
If emptiness were without the sun, darkness would never be dispelled.
The sun of wisdom is also like this.
If the nature of the mind were empty, how could it have anything to illuminate?
If the nature of the mind were empty and lacked wisdom, delusions and afflictions would never be severed;
they would be like darkness, having neither coming nor going.
The sun also neither arises nor ceases;
the same is true for delusion and awakening.
It is only by way of conventional designation that one speaks of "destroying delusion."
The nature of delusion is non-existent;
it neither comes nor goes, and truly there is nothing to be destroyed.
Although wisdom shines universally, [it finds no object].
Its nature is eternally quiescent;
it neither arises nor ceases, and ultimately there is nothing to be illuminated.
It is like when the sun shines upon the sky, and heaven and earth become brilliantly clear.
When one turns back to contemplate that the nature of the mind is empty,
then all phenomena of the mundane world and all supramundane phenomena are clearly and perfectly revealed.
For this reason:
It is taught that wisdom illuminates the nature of the mind,
like the sun in the sky.
If one can investigate these ten similes of the sun in the sky, [one will realize this].
One penetrates the characteristics of all phenomena;
by means of this, one enters the ocean of awakened mind.
This is what is called "discriminating the characteristics of all phenomena."
2. Explanation of the Name "Samādhi of the Factors of Enlightenment" (Bodhyaṅga-samādhi). This is the second [section]. Question:
What is meant by the name "Samādhi of the Factors of Enlightenment"?
And what is "intention" (manas)?
Because the Bodhisattva awakens to this mind,
he immediately attains the perfection of samādhi;
furthermore, all dharmas are immeasurable.
Why is it that one clarifies samādhi by means of mental application and awareness?
The answer is:
"Awareness" (saṃbodha) means clear illumination and thorough understanding.
"Mind" refers to the various primary minds and mental factors;
"samādhi" refers to the concentration of being disciplined and straight.
When the practitioner's various primary minds and mental factors arise, [they are brought into this state].
When one reflects back and observes, no movement or shifting is perceived.
For this reason, it is called the Samādhi of Awakened Mind.
As it was asked:
All phenomena are immeasurable. Why,
then, is it that only those corresponding to the mental faculty are used to clarify samādhi through awakening,
while others are not discussed?
Answer: Although all phenomena are indeed immeasurable,
when their ultimate source is investigated,
there are none that are not created by the mind, intellect, and consciousness.
The reason for this is that some say:
if there is initial awareness upon encountering an object.
That which differs from wood and stone is called the mind (*citta*).
That which subsequently deliberates and discriminates is called the intellect (*manas*).
That which clearly cognizes and comprehends is termed consciousness (*vijñāna*).
This is the distinction between mind (citta), thought (manas),
and consciousness (vijñāna). One who grasps in such a manner falls into the inversion of mind.
Within the inversion of perception and the inversion of view,
if one can understand that within the mind there is neither intention nor non-intention,
then within the mind there is neither consciousness nor non-consciousness.
If within the mind there is neither the existence of mind nor the non-existence of mind,
then within the mind there is neither the existence of consciousness nor the non-existence of consciousness.
If within consciousness there is neither intention nor non-intention,
then within consciousness there is neither mind nor non-mind.
This mind, intellect,
and consciousness are designated by three names because they are not one;
yet they are said to be of a single nature because they are not three.
If names were not names,
then natures would likewise not be natures;
because they are not names, they are not three.
Because they lack intrinsic nature, they are not one;
because they are not three, they do not combine;
because they are not one, they do not disperse.
Because it is not combined, it does not exist;
because it is not dispersed, it is not empty;
because it is not existent, it is not eternal.
Because it is not empty, it is not subject to annihilation;
therefore, mind, thought, and consciousness are neither annihilated nor eternal.
If one does not perceive annihilation or eternity, one will ultimately not perceive unity or difference.
Therefore, what is called "mind" (manas) encompasses the meaning of both "heart" (citta) and "consciousness" (vijñāna).
All phenomena are likewise so.
If one can observe with a profound mind,
then the ignorance of the mental faculty (*manas*) being destroyed, all other latent tendencies of delusion (*moha-anuśaya*) will also be extinguished accordingly.
Although these dharmas are numerous, [they are thus overcome].
However, by raising the point of "awakening the mind" (jueyi), one clarifies samādhi;
its meaning is so comprehensive that there is nothing it does not encompass.
Furthermore, as it is said in the sūtras:
What is called the bodhyaṅga-samādhi?
Among all samādhis, because one attains the seven factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅgas), it is named the bodhyaṅga-samādhi.
Regarding what is called "all samādhis," all dharmas are indeed samādhi,
because all dharmas are from the beginning eternally quiescent and immovable.
Furthermore, to speak briefly of samādhi,
there are three types:
the first is the mundane.
Second is the supramundane;
third is the supreme-supramundane.
Regarding "worldly samādhi":
This refers to the ten universal mental factors (mahābhūmika) within the distracted mind of the desire realm,
as well as the meditative absorption of the desire realm and the preparatory stage (anāgamya).
The four dhyānas,
the four immeasurable minds,
and the four formless attainments.
Supramundane samādhi refers to the liberations (vimokṣa) and the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana).
The ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*),
the nine successive attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*),
and the lion’s bound (*siṃhavijṛmbhita*).
These include the practices of transcendence and equality,
the contemplation of refinement through cultivation,
and up to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment within the practice of wisdom.
The three gates of liberation,
the four noble truths,
the twelve links of dependent origination, and other samādhis.
The supramundane, most excellent samādhi refers to the samādhi of the lineage of the ten powers,
the Śūraṅgama and other one hundred and eight samādhis.
Up to as many samādhis as there are atoms in the worlds of the ten directions—
these are the three kinds of samāpatti that encompass all dharmas.
Since these are all dharmas, they are called the various samādhis.
How are they named the seven factors of enlightenment?
As for the seven factors of enlightenment:
First, the awakening factor of discrimination;
second, the awakening factor of energy;
third, the awakening factor of joy.
4. The awakening factor of investigation of phenomena;
5. The awakening factor of equanimity;
6. The awakening factor of concentration.
The seven factors of enlightenment;
these constitute the seven awakenings.
The meaning of the seven awakenings has many aspects.
To summarize and clarify briefly, these do not exceed six types. What are the six?
The first is hearing about the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).
Second, the seven factors of enlightenment of cultivation;
third, the seven factors of enlightenment of realizing principle;
fourth, the seven factors of enlightenment of initiating skillful means.
Fifth is entering the dharma-gate of the seven factors of enlightenment;
sixth is the ultimate perfection of the seven factors of enlightenment.
Regarding the first, [the stage] of hearing the seven factors of enlightenment:
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty and quiescent, ultimately pure;
yet, sentient beings are unable to know this.
If they encounter Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or spiritual friends who explain that all phenomena are originally empty and quiescent, [they may then understand].
Upon hearing this, the person was immediately struck with great awakening.
Consequently, they thoroughly understood the mind and all phenomena, all *samādhis*, and their ultimate purity,
emptiness, and non-existence, thereby attaining the seven factors of enlightenment.
Because this person develops [the awakening factors] by means of hearing,
they are called the "seven factors of awakening through hearing.
Second are those who practice the seven factors of awakening.
If a practitioner,
although knowing that the mind and all phenomena within all samādhis are empty and devoid of arising or ceasing,
still gives rise to inverted perceptions.
In accordance with whatever thoughts arise,
one should always use the seven factors of enlightenment to bring them into harmony;
cultivate the mind through inward reflection and observation.
By means of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) to bring about harmony and adaptability,
one then suddenly and completely awakens to the mind, all phenomena, and all *samādhis*.
From the very beginning, it is neither born nor extinguished, like Great Nirvana;
this is what is called the cultivation of the seven factors of enlightenment.
Third, the seven factors of enlightenment that accord with principle:
If a person, by means of these two causal conditions— the practice of faith and the practice of the Dharma—
awakens to the mind and all phenomena as being, in principle, identical to True Suchness (tathatā), they attain all samādhis.
Yet one knows that even true suchness (tathatā) is not [inherently] true suchness.
If one awakens to true suchness,
then regarding the principle of true suchness, one possesses the seven factors of enlightenment (saptabodhyaṅga).
Therefore, one does not dwell in the realization of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
This is what is called the seven factors of enlightenment that accord with principle.
Fourth is the arising of the seven factors of enlightenment through skillful means (*upāya*).
If a practitioner attains the principle of non-realization yet gives rise to a mind of compassion for sentient beings and engages in the myriad practices,
they know that whatever they perform is entirely quiescent.

Although they know there is neither abiding nor practice, through the skillful means of the seven factors of enlightenment, they cultivate all samādhi practices for the benefit of both self and others.
It is like planting a tree in mid-air;
this is called the arousal of the seven factors of enlightenment through skillful means.
Fifth is the entry into the dharma-gate of the seven factors of enlightenment.
If a bodhisattva can thus not rely on the mind or any phenomena—
whether they be ultimate or conventional—
in all samādhis, this constitutes the fulfillment of the contemplation of the two emptinesses.
One attains entry into the Middle Way.
By simultaneously illuminating the two truths according to what the mind contemplates,
all samādhis and the various lineages of the ten powers naturally arise.
Furthermore, one does not apprehend the characteristics of the various samādhis. Why is this?
Because all dhāraṇīs and the characteristics of all dhāraṇīs are empty.
Because all samādhis and the characteristics of all samādhis are empty,
the mind has no dwelling or attachment amidst the merits and wisdom of all dhāraṇīs and samādhis.
This constitutes the Bodhisattva’s complete manifestation of each of the seven factors of enlightenment;
therefore, it is called "entering the Dharma-gate of the seven enlightenments" and is also termed "opening the Buddha's knowledge and vision."
If one can open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision,
then mind after mind will be quiescent and extinguished,
naturally flowing into [enlightenment].

Within the pure meditations of the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten stages, and the stage of equal enlightenment, one thus attains the name of "entering the Dharma-gate of the seven factors of enlightenment. Regarding the sixth, the perfect and ultimate seven factors of enlightenment:
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in the pure meditation of the vajra-samādhi,
they will attain clear and great awakening, realizing the wisdom of a single thought-instant of correspondence.
In tranquil stillness, there is perfect illumination, with all things clearly and distinctly perceived;
this is called the ultimate perfection of the seven factors of enlightenment,
and it is also called the unsurpassed wondrous enlightenment.
It is also called the seven factors of enlightenment of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Because of such meanings of the seven factors of enlightenment,
from the first production of the thought of enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda*), the bodhisattva...
All methods of contemplative practice ultimately culminate in the fruit of enlightenment and are collectively termed the seven factors of awakening;
they are also called the observation of the characteristics of the mind.
It is also called the "reflexively illuminating consciousness.
Such various names as these refer to immeasurable samādhis;
in the language of Qin, it means "to harmonize and straighten the mind."
It is also called the Samādhi of Constant Quiescence.
It is like a bright mirror that does not move, or still water without waves;
yet when confronted with various objects, it reflects them all.
All images appear therein;
the mind is likewise.
Although its nature is luminous and pure, [it reflects all things].
Because the mind is moved by discursive thought,
there is no clear illumination; therefore,
one should practice based on what precedes it.
He immediately attained the Samādhi of the Universal Manifestation of the Dharma-gate of Immovable Mindfulness.
Having attained this concentration, he...
When the mind is free from crookedness and deviousness,
it is called samādhi; therefore,
it is termed the "Samādhi of Awakened Mind."
3. Explanation of the Practice of the Skillful Means for the Bodhyanga-samādhi. Explanation of the Practice of the Skillful Means for the Bodhyanga-samādhi, Part Three. Question:
The name and meaning of the bodhyanga-samādhi have already been understood as such.
By practicing what skillful means does the practitioner attain this samādhi?
Within all samādhis, they attain the seven factors of enlightenment;
entering the profound nature of phenomena, they reach great parinirvāṇa.
One attains permanence, bliss, self, and purity,
and acts as a supreme island for all sentient beings.
He replied:
In order to accomplish great compassion and deliver sentient beings,
the practitioner seeks the unsurpassed Bodhi, the path of ultimate truth;
first, they should establish a great vow.
I give rise to a heart of sincere resolve and make this solemn vow:
if that which I study is not accomplished,
I shall never midway harbor regret or a mind of despondency and retreat.
At that time, the mind is like a vajra;
with resolute conviction, one knows that all phenomena are ultimately empty and quiescent,
yet one does not abandon infinite sentient beings.
Therefore, one cultivates all practices.
What is meant by cultivation?
It is when a practitioner thoroughly understands the mind and all phenomena.
All are non-existent, neither arising nor ceasing;
they are quiescent and pure,
yet are able to skillfully employ the expedient means of the six perfections.
By means of this, one subdues the deluded mind;
once the deluded mind has ceased, samādhi arises spontaneously.
What are the six?
If a practitioner knows that the mind and its objects are like what is seen in a dream,
and that none of them possess any reality.
Therefore, one should be able to relinquish all that exists;
one should constantly maintain self-awareness so as not to allow thoughts of stinginess or attachment to arise.
Furthermore, one should dedicate this pure mind of renunciation.
Bestowing [it] universally upon all sentient beings;
at that time, it is called cultivating the mind of pure giving.
Because of this mind, [the merit is purified].
Then one can proceed toward the dānapāramitā.
If a practitioner knows that the mind is like an illusion,
all external unwholesome dharmas are found to be non-existent.
Although one constantly maintains self-awareness amidst all sensory objects so as not to allow unwholesome thoughts to arise,
this state is called the cultivation of the mind of pure precepts.
Because of this mind, one is then able to advance toward the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
If the practitioner knows that the mind is like a flame— empty and without root— then they can proceed.
The eight external phenomena are likewise all devoid of reality.
Therefore, regarding gain and loss, defamation and praise, renown and insignificance, suffering and pleasure,
one should always maintain self-awareness and refrain from giving rise to attachment or aversion.
This is called cultivating firm patience;
by means of this mind,
one is then able to advance toward the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
If the practitioner knows that the mind is like a magical illusion and is constantly self-aware and awakened,
they observe the continuity of mental formations.
One does not allow thoughts of indolence or negligence to arise;
this state is called cultivating the mind of diligence (*vīrya*).
Because of this mind, one is able to advance toward the *pāramitā* of diligence (*vīryapāramitā*).
If a practitioner knows that the mind is like a reflection in a mirror,
such that all phenomena which serve as objects of focus are non-existent,
then throughout the four modes of conduct— walking, standing, sitting, and lying down— [they remain thus].
Distracted thoughts do not arise; even if mindfulness is momentarily lost, one immediately becomes aware of it.
Thus, the waves of delusion do not stir and the mind remains constantly tranquil.
At this time, it is called cultivating the pure concentrated mind.
By means of this mind,
one is able to advance toward the dhyāna-pāramitā;
if the practitioner understands that the mind is like empty space.
The internal and external phenomena that serve as objects for the six consciousnesses are all non-existent;
they are ultimately empty and quiescent.
Skillfully employing the mind of non-apprehension, one destroys all inversions;
one does not apprehend any phenomena and does not cling to any phenomena.
To fully comprehend all phenomena—
this is what is called cultivating the mind of right wisdom.
It is because of this mind that [one attains liberation].
Thus one is able to advance toward the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If a practitioner does not cultivate the six kinds of pure minds directed toward the path as described above,
they will be incapable of practicing the profound samādhi.
Therefore, those who wish to cultivate the samādhi of the factors of enlightenment must skillfully study the aforementioned expedient means of the six perfections.
These six expedient means encompass all expedient means.
If one can skillfully employ the mind of subduing the six obscurations to make the will supple,
and subsequently observe with careful, discerning, and subtle attention to enter the gateway of right wisdom,
this is called the preliminary skillful means for practicing the profound samādhi.
4. Explanation of the Mind-Characteristics of the Bodhyanga-samādhi. Explanation of the Mind-Characteristics of the Bodhyanga-samādhi, Part Four. Question:
How does a practitioner wish to enter this samādhi?
One should observe the characteristics of several types of mind.
The answer is:
the characteristics of the mind are explained in various sūtras and śāstras.
The various differences between them are not described in detail here.
Within this, four types of mental characteristics are briefly clarified to serve as the objects of contemplation. What are these four?
First, non-recollection;
second, the desire for recollection;
third, recollection.
Fourth, regarding "having already recollected":
"not yet having recollected" means the mind has not yet arisen to take an object as its condition;
"desiring to recollect" means the mind desires to arise and take an object as its condition.
"Mindfulness" refers to the mind abiding fully while taking an object as its condition.
"Having mindfulness" refers to the mind having already completed its full satisfaction while taking an object as its condition and having subsequently ceased. Question:
The characteristics of the mind are manifold.
Why, then, are only these four modes of mental activity mentioned?
The answer is as follows:
These four modes of mental application encompass all states of mind;
for example, as when one is directed toward unwholesome phenomena or has not yet thought of unwholesome phenomena.
He conceives thoughts of unwholesome dharmas;
he contemplates unwholesome dharmas; having contemplated unwholesome dharmas, [he becomes remorseful].
Just as when one contemplates wholesome phenomena,
one has not yet thought of the wholesome,
but desires to think of the wholesome.
Mindfulness of the wholesome. Having practiced mindfulness of the wholesome,
one takes as objects all afflictions, such as the six sense-objects and the three poisons.
Even in walking, standing, sitting,
or reclining; in speech, eating, drinking, and all activities performed,
there is at all times the mind characterized by these four aspects mentioned above.
Furthermore, all minds that take the various phenomena of the world as their objects possess these four characteristics; therefore,
only these four types of characteristics are taught.
[He] considered that there is no object of observation not encompassed [by this].
He asked: "What is meant by 'characteristics'?
He replied:
That which can be grasped and distinguished is called a "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*).
Since the dharmas of mind and consciousness possess no physical form or substance,
they would be difficult to comprehend if not analyzed through these four modes of mental activity.
If it cannot be clearly understood, it cannot be observed;
therefore, one must first distinguish it by means of the four characteristics.
If one observes with clarity and thorough penetration, one realizes that these characteristics are not [inherently existent] characteristics.
One immediately enters into the equality of the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇasamatā*).
It is asked: "Regarding the contemplation of desire-thoughts (*kāmacitta*), it may be so that one contemplates the characteristics of the two movements of the mind."
When there is no thought and nothing has arisen, it is the state of no-mind.
Because there is no mind, there are no characteristics to be discriminated.
Having reflected thus:
that which has already ceased is no different from non-existence;
the absence of phenomena is itself the absence of marks.
How should it be observed?
The answer is:
although it has not yet arisen, it exists even before it is brought to mind.
Yet it is not that there is ultimately no mind. Why is this?
It is, for example, like a person who has not yet acted.
When there is a subsequent matter requiring action, one should simply perform it;
one cannot claim that because something has not yet been done,
no person exists.
If there were definitely no person,
who would subsequently perform the act?
For there exists a person who has not yet performed it.
Thus, for a person who arises later,
the characteristics of the mind should likewise be so,
because the prior thought has not yet occurred.
Desire-thought can arise only if there is no mind that has not yet thought;
how could desire-thought exist otherwise?
Therefore, although that which has not yet been thought has not yet arisen,
one cannot say that it is ultimately non-existent.
As for what you said:
As for the claim that "once mindfulness has ceased, it can no longer be observed," this is also not the case;
even though mindfulness has ceased, it can still be observed.
For example, when a person has completed a task,
one cannot say that there is no person;
if it were definitively the case that there is no person, [the task could not have been accomplished].
Who was it that previously acted?
Upon reflection, one finds that the mind likewise ceases;
yet one cannot say that it is eternally extinguished and devoid of mind.
If the mind, once extinguished, were to be extinguished forever,
that would be the view of annihilationism,
which asserts the non-existence of cause and effect.
Therefore, even though mindfulness has already ceased,
it can still be observed.
Question:
How do you contemplate the mind?
If you contemplate the past mind,
the past mind has already passed away.
If one contemplates the future mind, the future mind has not yet arrived;
if one contemplates the present mind, the present mind does not abide.
Apart from these three periods of time, there is no separate mind.
Furthermore, what kind of mind is being observed?
The answer is:
Your question is incorrect.
If the past has been eternally extinguished and is ultimately unknowable,
how can the noble ones know all past minds?
If the future mind has not yet arrived, does not exist, and is unknowable, [how can they know it]?
How is it that the noble ones can know all future minds?
If the present mind does not abide and cannot be known,
how do the noble ones [know them]?
They are able to know all matters currently being thought of by sentient beings throughout the ten directions,
just as worldly spirits and deities do.
If one is already able to know the minds of one's own three periods of existence and can also know the minds of others across the three periods of existence,
how could such a person not be a practitioner of the Buddha-dharma?
And they give rise to the view of annihilation,
claiming that the mind of the three periods of time is like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit.
It cannot be known.
One should understand that although the minds of the three periods of time lack fixed reality, [they nevertheless exist].
This can also be understood.
Thus, a verse says:
"That which has been taught by all the Buddhas."
Though empty, it is not annihilated;
though continuous, it is not eternal;
and yet, neither demerit nor merit is lost.
Do not sever your vision and remain in a state of ignorance;
do not fail to cultivate meditative practice like one who is blind,
for though facing various forms, you would see nothing at all.
You are likewise;
within the Buddha-dharma, you lack the eye of right contemplation and thus gain nothing from emptiness.
5. Explanation of the Entrance to Contemplation through the Samādhi of the Factors of Enlightenment (Bodhyaṅga). Question:
We have already understood the characteristics of the mind during its four modes of activity.
It encompasses all states of mind.
How does the practitioner observe this mind?
By penetrating the true nature and illuminating it perfectly.
It is clear that all samādhis are endowed with the seven factors of enlightenment.
The answer says:
First, the practitioner adorns themselves with great vows.
One should skillfully cultivate the aforementioned dharma-gates of the six perfections to harmonize the mind,
and with faith understand that all phenomena are ultimately empty and quiescent.
Yet I am shrouded by ignorance and have not yet attained awakening;
I must diligently cultivate right contemplation,
for it is only upon reaching the destination that one knows.
How could one allow empty-minded, false interpretations to bring about self-destruction?
Once you have been able to skillfully harmonize yourself,
you may then act according to whatever arises in the mind.
With a mind free from dwelling or attachment,
one turns back to reflectively observe the characteristics of the thought that has not yet arisen, the thought that is currently arising, and the thought that has already ceased.
At that time, one clearly observes that the thought which has not yet arisen is ceasing.
When a thought of desire arises in the mind,
the mind that has not yet thought does not cease;
a thought of desire arises in the mind.
When the mind of non-intention arises,
the mind of intention is neither extinguished nor not extinguished;
thus the mind of intention arises.
Thus, regarding the four propositions concerning non-arising,
one observes that both the desire for thought and the arising of thought are unattainable.
If the desire for thought and the arising of thought are unattainable, then neither their arising nor their non-arising can be attained.
One thereby attains liberation within the nature of the mind. How is it that,
regarding the four propositions concerning what has not yet been thought,
one observes that the arising of a mind of desire cannot be apprehended?
First, regarding the initial phrase "not yet thought," one observes that the arising of a mind with desire cannot be apprehended.
If it is claimed that a mind with desire arises because the unthought mind has ceased, [then...]
When the mind that has not yet thought has already ceased, where does the thought of desire arise?
Does it arise immediately upon the cessation of that non-thought,
or does it arise apart from the cessation of that non-thought?
If one were to give rise to a desire-thought immediately upon the cessation of an unarisen thought,
then that dharma which has ceased should not arise;
for arising and ceasing are mutually contradictory in their essential natures.
If it is claimed that arising exists within cessation itself,
and that arising and cessation are not mutually contradictory,
this is not the case.
If that were so, it would be like a ripe fruit: within the rind there is a seed;
when the rind decays, the seed emerges.
The rind is not the seed, and the seed is not the rind.
How could the peel be identical to the kernel?
The mental phenomena are also like this:
once extinguished, they cannot arise again.
Therefore, it is impossible for a mind of desire to arise when that which has not yet ceased through non-attention is present.
If one were to claim that a mind of desire arises apart from that which has not yet ceased through non-attention,
then its arising would be without cause.
This is not so. Since arising has no source from which it arises, it is not called "arising.
It is like space, which has no source from which it arises.
Therefore, space is not called "arising.
One should know that apart from the mind that has not yet been thought of or that has already ceased, a mind of desire cannot be found.
It is the same for the practitioner.
Whether in the state of identity or separation,
one observes that the cessation of the unarisen thought and the arising of the thought of desire are ultimately unattainable.
Second, to clarify the second phrase regarding the non-arising of a mind of desire when there is no prior thought:
if one claims that a mind of desire arises even though the prior mind has not ceased, [this is untenable].
Does arising occur as that which is not-ceasing,
or does it occur apart from that which is not-ceasing?
If arising occurs as that which is not-ceasing, then that which is not-ceasing would itself be arising.
How could this arising give rise [to itself]?
If this arising were able to give rise to this very arising,
there would have to be yet another arising.
If origination were to originate, there would be an infinite series of originations.
This is not the case if this "origination of origination" is of the same nature as the primary origination.
If it were of one and the same substance, [the fault of infinite regress would follow].
Within a single [entity], there should not be multiple productions;
just as within a single finger there are no multiple fingers.
If they were produced as distinct entities, [this would be the case].
Then it should not be called "arising," because arising is distinguished by its own essential nature and cannot produce itself.
Just as the substances of peach and crabapple are distinct:
a peach does not produce a crabapple,
and a crabapple does not produce a peach.
Therefore, the non-extinction of the unarisen thought cannot be found within the arising of a thought of desire;
nor can it be said that the non-extinction of the unarisen thought exists apart from it.
Regarding those for whom thoughts of desire arise:
from where do these thoughts of desire arise?
If they arise, they arise from nowhere.
This would mean arising without a cause.

If something were to arise without a cause, it would not be an arising at all; yet to speak of an arising that is not an arising is untenable, as it falls into the error of denying both cause and effect.
As it is said regarding the son of a barren woman or the child of a eunuch,
one should know that apart from the non-arising and non-ceasing of thought,
a mind with desire cannot be found to exist.
The practitioner is likewise:
whether in the state of union or separation,
they observe that the unarisen thought does not cease.
The thought of desire arises in the mind,
yet ultimately it cannot be apprehended.
Regarding the third line, the three knowledges (vidyā) pertain to that which has not yet been thought.
When one observes the mind that gives rise to a thought of desire, it cannot be apprehended.
If one were to say that even a mind that has not yet conceived a thought is both ceasing and not ceasing,
such that there exists a mind that gives rise to a thought of desire—
If that which exists also perishes, why need it not also be unperishing?
If that which exists does not perish, why need it also perish?
For an indeterminate cause cannot produce a determinate result.
Just as one with indeterminate faculties cannot produce a child with determinate faculties,
so too it would be if one were to say that [the self] both ceases and does not cease.
Because their essence is one and without difference,
it is not the case that there is the arising of a mind with desire;
rather, it both ceases and does not cease.
Nor is it both non-extinguished and extinguished;
because their natures are contradictory, they cannot be a single entity.
Nor can that which is not different [from them] give rise to desire and thought.
Just as a person with indeterminate faculties cannot produce a single child because the two faculties are not a single entity,
so too, if one were to claim that the entities of "extinguished" and "not extinguished" are distinct, [the same fault would apply].
Regarding the statement that "each of the two can give rise to desire-thought":
if their substance were different, they would simply be cessation and non-cessation.
Since it is definitively not cessation, how could it be called both cessation and non-cessation?
If both that which is definitely extinguished and that which is definitely not extinguished were each capable of producing a desire-thought,
then two desire-thoughts would necessarily arise simultaneously.
In reality, this is not so.
If neither of the two were to arise, then no thought of desire would arise.
When the practitioner contemplates in this manner, [desire does not arise].
The unarisen thought is neither extinguished nor non-extinguished;
the arising of a mind through volitional thought is ultimately unobtainable.
Next, the fourth phrase is explained in relation to the unarisen thought.
When one observes the mind that gives rise to a thought of desire, it cannot be apprehended.

If one were to claim that the mind which has not yet given rise to the thought is neither extinguished nor non-extinguished, and that there exists a mind that gives rise to the thought of desire; [this is untenable].
If a cause produces that which is not subject to cessation,
it need not be non-cessation;
if a cause produces that which is not non-cessation, [it need not be cessation].
Then it would not be necessary for [the object] to be negated by non-destruction; for since that which is non-destructive and that which is not non-destructive are distinct from what they negate,
they should not both be taken together as causes.
This is also a cause of contradiction,
because they cannot share a single result,
just as water and fire are mutually exclusive.
In the end, no fruit will ever arise therein.
If it is claimed that production occurs because both causes are non-existent,
this is not the case.
If that which is not the locus of the two were each to exist,
then those two existences would in turn give rise to two further births; however,
in reality, this is not so.
If both [the producer and the produced] were non-existent in their respective places,
then there would be no capacity for production;
how then could that which produces give rise to that which is produced?
If there were neither the producer nor the produced,
then that which is produced could not be called "produced," because that which is produced would have no source from which it arises.
The practitioner contemplates in this way that there is neither cessation nor non-cessation;
the mind arising from the thought of desire is ultimately unattainable.
Furthermore, since the practitioner has already been able to apply this analysis to the first set of four propositions regarding the movement of the initial thought:
Contemplate that the arising of a thought of desire is unattainable.
Having done so, one should then return to the fourfold analysis of the arising of a thought of desire and contemplate it further.
Contemplate that the ceasing of a thought that has not yet arisen is unattainable.
What is contemplation?
If one considers that the unarisen mind is what ceases,
it is for the purpose of giving rise to the arisen mind so that the unarisen mind may cease.
One desires that the thought of recollection does not arise and the thought of non-recollection ceases;
one desires that the thought of recollection both arises and does not arise and the thought of non-recollection ceases;
one desires that the thought of recollection neither arises nor does not arise and the thought of non-recollection ceases.
In this way, returning once more, one investigates within the fourfold propositions regarding the thought of desire until the unarisen mind is extinguished;
ultimately, the characteristics of such investigation cannot be found, and thus one turns back to apply the same analysis to the fourfold propositions regarding the unarisen [mind].
Contemplate the category of mental verbalizations regarding desire as being subtle and composed of their own constituent parts, and so forth.
If the practitioner does not perceive the arising and ceasing of the mind that has not yet conceived a thought of desire...
Then it must necessarily be arising and ceasing;
it must be both arising and ceasing and neither arising nor ceasing;
it must be neither arising and ceasing nor neither arising nor ceasing.
It is merely because ordinary beings, through their inverted delusions,
conceive of arising and ceasing— even up to non-arising and non-ceasing— within all dharmas and within thoughts that have not yet arisen.
They are not non-arising and non-ceasing;
they are deceptive and lack reality,
being entirely unobtainable and existing as mere names.
The dharma of names does not exist within, without, or between the two; nor does it exist eternally of itself.
This is precisely the absence of names.
If one does not apprehend the names of the four positions, such as arising and ceasing, [then names do not exist].
Nor can one obtain the absence of names.
Because names cannot be obtained, it is not provisional;
because the absence of names cannot be obtained, it is not empty.
Because it cannot be grasped as substantial, it is not the conventional;
because it cannot be grasped as empty, it is not the ultimate;
because it cannot be grasped as conventional, it is not the mundane.
Because it does not attain the supramundane, it is not supramundane;
because it does not attain the mundane, it is not with outflows (*sāsrava*);
because it does not attain the supramundane, it is not without outflows (*anāsrava*).
Because it cannot be attained as contaminated, it is not saṃsāra;
because it cannot be attained as uncontaminated, it is not nirvāṇa.
When the practitioner contemplates in this way, even before a thought of desire arises, [they see it thus].
If one does not perceive the two extremes, one will not grasp at the two extremes.
If one does not grasp at the two extremes, one will not cling to them to give rise to various fetters and karmic actions.
If there are no obstructions or coverings from the fetters and karmic actions of the two extremes, [one is liberated].
The mind of correct contemplation is like space, profound and pure.
By means of this Middle Way right wisdom,
it is brilliantly awakened, illuminating both truths simultaneously.
Mind after mind becomes tranquil and naturally flows into the great ocean of *nirvāṇa*.

If one observes a thought that has not yet arisen or a thought of desire, the same applies to all subsequent thoughts and all categories of mental factors (*citta-dharma*). This should be understood accordingly.
This is a brief explanation of the characteristics of right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*).
Furthermore, there are two kinds of practicing right contemplation: first, general contemplation (*samudāyālambana*);
[second, specific contemplation].
Second is the sequential and distinct contemplation.
Regarding the first-mentioned general contemplation:
if the practitioner does not yet possess the power of great skillful means, [they should practice this].
Because one cannot observe the true nature in all places,
one should first illuminate and understand the mind within seated meditation;
this is called the general contemplation of the mind.
The reason the second is called "distinctive contemplation" (*pṛthag-vipaśyanā*) is that if a practitioner,
through skillful means, is able to constantly apply the mind to all objects,
this is a distinctive contemplation of the mind and mental factors.
Furthermore, when a practitioner wishes to enter samādhi,
they must first observe the mind and mental factors within their seat;
thereafter, they should likewise observe the mind and mental factors in all places.
Why is this? Among the four modes of deportment,
it is only during the act of sitting that the body and mind are tranquil, neither sinking nor floating.
Because it does not arise from conditions other than itself, the mind possesses the contemplation of phenomena as they truly are.
Thus, a sutra says:
"Sit upright and contemplate the true mark."
This is called the first repentance.
Therefore, a practitioner should first cultivate samādhi in a secluded room or a quiet chamber.
What is cultivation?
The practitioner should skillfully harmonize their own body and mind;
every detail is as explained in the dhyāna methods.
This should be explained in detail herein.
When the practitioner has been able to properly harmonize themselves,
at that time they should remain within their seat.
Through right mindfulness, one observes that the meanings of the four movements of mind, intellect,
and consciousness are entirely unobtainable.
The analytical deconstruction through contemplative practice is entirely as described above.
At this time, it is called practicing samādhi within seated meditation.
In this way, the practitioner realizes that mind, intellect, and consciousness are neither seen nor obtained.
Furthermore, one should attend accordingly to whatever activity is being performed,
observing the internal and external mind with single-minded clarity.
The external mind is termed the "agent."
The internal mind is called the experiencer.
In the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*,
it speaks of both the agent and the experiencer.
The practitioner contemplates the agent through six matters;
they contemplate the recipient through six kinds;
contemplating both the internal and external together constitutes twelve kinds.
This samādhi-object can give rise to samādhi.
The practitioner should observe it according to the place where it arises.
Regarding the six external [objects]:
That is to say:
first, practice;
second, abiding.
Third, sitting;
fourth, lying down;
fifth, performing activities.
Sixth, discursive speech.
Regarding the six internal sensations,
they are as follows:
First, the eye perceives forms;
second, the ear perceives sounds;
third, the nose perceives odors.
Fourth, the tongue experiences tastes;
fifth, the body experiences tangibles;
sixth, the mind takes dharmas as its object.
These are the twelve objects of contemplation,
which are the gateways to samādhi.
First, regarding the time of walking:
One should then observe within the course of practice whether one has not yet practiced or is about to practice.
They practice.
Having practiced,
their minds penetrate one another, yet all are ultimately ungraspable.
The dual illumination is as clear as previously described.
Furthermore, one reflects:
"Such movement exists because it is driven and directed by the mind; thus, there is coming and going."
When one turns back to observe the mind that practices, no place of abiding is seen;
there is neither arising nor ceasing, nor any characteristics whatsoever.
One should know that the practitioner is ultimately empty and quiescent.
Second, if it were in a state of abiding,
one should then clearly observe that it has not yet abided.
He wishes to abide;
he abides;
having abided.
The characteristics of the mind are all unapprehendable.
The dual illumination is clear and distinct, as fully explained previously.
Furthermore, one forms this thought:
One who abides in this manner is said to "abide" because they control the mind and maintain the body erect and settled; yet,
when looking back at the abiding mind, no location for it is perceived.
How much more so regarding all marks of arising and ceasing;
one should know that that which abides is ultimately empty and quiescent.
Third, while sitting, one should immediately observe with clear discernment.
Not yet seated;
about to sit; seated.
Having sat down,
the characteristics of the mind are all ungraspable;
the dual illumination is as clear and distinct as previously described.
Again, he thought: "As for this act of sitting,
it is called 'sitting' because the body is settled by turning the mind and bending the legs."
Looking back at the seated mind, one does not perceive arising or ceasing, nor is it internal or external;
one should know that that which sits is ultimately empty and quiescent.
Fourth, during the time of sleep:
One should then observe with clear attention whether one has not yet fallen asleep or is about to fall asleep.
He falls asleep.
Having fallen asleep,
the characteristics of the mind are all unapprehendable.
The clear, dual illumination is also as described above.
Furthermore, he reflects:
"Such is the nature of sleep."
Due to the exhaustion of the mind,
one immediately relinquishes the six sense faculties and lies down prostrate;
therefore, it is called sleep.
Looking back at the mind while asleep, one does not perceive its characteristics;
one should know that sleep is ultimately empty and quiescent.
Fifth, if [the mind] is active, one should immediately observe it with clear attention.
Not yet done; about to be done; being done.
Once it has been performed,
the characteristics of the mind are all unattainable;
the clear, simultaneous illumination is also as explained above.
Again, he reflects:
"Now, when I move my hands and body to perform various activities,
the raising and lowering of the hands are directed by the mind."
Because it accomplishes various tasks, it is called "action.
When one turns back to observe the mind that acts, no movement or shifting is seen;
one should know that the agent is ultimately empty and quiescent.
When the sixth practitioner is reading or reciting words,
they should immediately observe them with clarity before speaking.
He wished to speak;
he spoke; having spoken, [he was silent].
The characteristics of the mind are all unattainable.
The clear, simultaneous illumination of both [aspects] is also as explained above.
Furthermore, he forms this thought:
Such sounds, whatever is spoken or uttered,
arise from the mind’s vitarka and vicāra;
they agitate the vital breaths, which then strike against the six sense bases.
It is because of the throat, lips, tongue, teeth, and palate that such speech exists.
When one turns back to examine the mind of speech, no trace is found; sound abides in emptiness.
One should know that speech is ultimately empty and quiescent.
This constitutes the practitioner’s sixfold contemplation of the external mind;
knowing them all to be empty and quiescent, one perceives no agent,
yet there exists a determinate, real characteristic.
Therefore, in all matters, the bodhisattva practices samādhi; thus,
it is said in the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra:
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when walking, knows that he is walking,
and so on, up to when sitting, knows that he is sitting."
When lying down, speaking, or wearing the saṃghāṭī robe,
he knows that all these are ultimately unobtainable;
therefore, this is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates that within the internal mind there are six kinds of feeling,
yet knows that there is no feeler.
Why is this so? Although all sensations are empty, if they are not investigated,
they can act as the causes and conditions for immeasurable afflictions and the cycle of birth and death.
Therefore, the practitioner should,
at the time when these various faculties encounter their respective objects,
observe each one individually.
How does one observe? When a practitioner of the first stage sees forms with the eye,
they should immediately observe them with clear discernment.
Not yet having seen forms,
desiring to see forms,
seeing forms.
Having seen forms,
the characteristics of the four movements are all unobtainable;
the dual illumination is clear and distinct, as explained in detail above.
Again, he thought: "One who views in this way is without the characteristic of viewing."
Why is this so? Because within those faculties, objects, emptiness, and clarity,
each is devoid of seeing and devoid of discrimination.
Through the conjunction of causes and conditions, visual consciousness arises.
With visual consciousness as a condition, mental consciousness arises.
When mental consciousness emerges:
One is then able to discern various forms;
furthermore, based upon the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), there arises visual consciousness (cakṣurvijñāna).
Through the causal conditions of visual consciousness, one is able to see forms.
Consequently, attachment arises.
Therefore, one should immediately turn back to contemplate the mind that perceives form.
When observing in this way, one does not see this mind coming from outside and entering.
And while experiencing [sensations],
one likewise does not see the mind emerging from within to produce discrimination. Why is this so?
External things have no concern with me;
if that which exists within me does not depend on causes and conditions,
one should know that the experiencer is ultimately empty and quiescent.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva Vimalakīrti said:
"The forms one perceives are equal to those seen by the blind.
Second, when a practitioner hears sounds with the ear, they should immediately observe them with clear discernment.
Not yet having heard a sound;
desiring to hear a sound;
hearing a sound.
Having heard these words,
the characteristics of the four movements were all found to be unobtainable;
the clear, simultaneous illumination of both aspects is explained in detail as above.
Again, he formed this thought:
"Such sounds as these have no intrinsic nature."
It arises solely from the conjunction of the sense faculties and their objects;
because it is the conceptualization and discrimination of the mental consciousness,
regarding what is heard.
When various afflictions and evil karmas arise,
one should immediately reflect back upon the consciousness that perceives sound;
its essential nature will not be found.
One should know that the hearer is ultimately empty and quiescent.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva Vimalakīrti said:
"The sounds one hears are equal to echoes."
Third, when the practitioner smells an odor with the nose,
they should immediately contemplate it with clear discernment:
"This is before the odor has been smelled."
Desiring to smell an odor,
one smells the odor;
having smelled the odor, [one reflects].
The minds of the four phases of movement are all ungraspable.
The clear illumination of both [aspects] is explained in detail as above.
Furthermore, he reflects thus:
Such fragrances are dharmas devoid of cognition;
the olfactory faculty itself is likewise fundamentally devoid of cognition.
Consciousness arises through the combination [of conditions];
it is conventionally designated as "knowing.
This is the false and illusory mental consciousness.
Having obtained what is experienced,
one gives rise to conceptual discrimination,
which initiates the various afflictions, the cycle of birth and death, and karmic activities.
One should immediately turn back and observe the mental consciousness;
seeing neither its source nor its characteristics,
one should know that the experiencer is ultimately empty and quiescent.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva Vimalakīrti said:
"The fragrance one smells is equal to the wind.
As for the fourth practitioner, when the tongue experiences flavors:
One should then observe with clarity:
"I have not yet experienced the flavor;
I desire to experience the flavor."
One experiences the flavor of sensation; having experienced the flavor of sensation,
the characteristics of the four movements are all unobtainable.
The clear illumination of both aspects has been explained in detail as above.
Furthermore, one reflects:
"In this way, the savoring of sensation truly lacks intrinsic nature."
Why is this? Because the six external tastes are without discrimination,
and the internal tongue-faculty is devoid of cognition.
However, it is only from the conjunction of causes and conditions that tongue-consciousness arises.
This consciousness is likewise not fixed within, without, or in between the two;
therefore, the central mind forcibly grasps the characteristics of taste.
Because one gives rise to attachment and discrimination,
all latent tendencies and afflictions exist;
at that time, one should immediately practice reflexive observation.
The mind, consciousness, and mental factors do not perceive a dwelling place within the attachment to flavors;
how much less could they perceive any characteristics of arising or ceasing?
One should know that it is the conceptualizing mind that clings to flavor.
"Because it is ultimately pure," the Bodhisattva Vimalakīrti said.
"One does not discriminate among the flavors of what is eaten."
When the practitioner of the fifth stage feels a tactile sensation with the body,
they should immediately observe it with discernment before the sensation is fully perceived.
He desires contact;
he experiences contact;
having experienced contact, [he reflects].
The characteristics of the four movements are all unattainable.
The clear, simultaneous illumination of both [aspects] is explained in detail as above.
Furthermore, he reflects thus:
Such awakening does not arise from within,
nor does it come from without.
Why is this? Because qualities such as cold, heat, softness,
and smoothness do not come from outside at all.
Since there is no distinct phenomenon that comes into being apart from cold, warmth, and so forth, the six parts of the body— such as the head and others— are not phenomena that arise. Therefore,
apart from these six parts of the body, there is likewise no phenomenon that arises.
When consciousness arises from the conjunction of these two,
it is termed "awareness. Furthermore,
the nature of this consciousness does not reside within or without.
Without any basis or support, one merely uses the mind and intention to forcibly construct discriminations,
claiming to realize various contacts.
Because one gives rise to perceptions of pleasure and pain,
there exist craving, aversion, and all afflictions.
At that time, one should immediately practice reflexive observation.
Conditioned by contact, the mind-consciousness does not perceive a place of abiding;
how much less so any characteristics of arising or ceasing?
One should know that this is the one capable of cognizing contact.
It is ultimately empty and quiescent;
therefore, the Bodhisattva Vimalakīrti said:
"One experiences all tactile sensations as if through the realization of wisdom."
When the practitioner of the sixth stage directs the mind toward dharmas,
they should immediately contemplate with discernment those dharmas not yet thought of.
He attends to the Dharma;
he attends to the Dharma; having attended to the Dharma, [he reflects upon it].
The mental characteristics of the four phases of movement are all ungraspable.
The clear, simultaneous illumination of both [aspects] is explained in detail as above.
Furthermore, one forms this thought:
In this way, the mental consciousness takes all phenomena as its objects, yet they are entirely deceptive and lack any substantial reality.
Why is this? Because the nature of phenomena is like an illusion or a magical transformation, lacking any reality;
and because the mind is like a mirage, never remaining still for even a moment.
Because phenomena have no fixed nature and cannot be taken as objects, the mind has no place of abiding; who, then, could be the subject that perceives?
Apart from the perceiving subject and the perceived object, there is no other perception.
You should know that it is solely through false conceptualization that one forcibly gives rise to the discrimination of dharmas, thereby producing various views; thus,
all afflictions, the cycle of birth and death, and karmic activities continue in succession without interruption.
Therefore, when the practitioner seeks to destroy false and inverted perceptions,
and when they encounter objects according to conditions, [they should apply this method].
One should immediately engage in reflexive observation.
In reflexively observing the source of mind, intellect, and consciousness,
when one observes the mind with discernment, one does not perceive any abiding, nor any arising or ceasing, nor any characteristics of phenomena.
If the mind has no place of abiding for the various marks of arising and ceasing,
one should know that this mind is unattainable;
since even the mind itself cannot be attained, how much less so the mental factors (caitta-dharma).
If there were no mental factors (*caitasika*), upon what would all phenomena ultimately depend?
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"My mind is itself empty; sin and merit have no master."
All phenomena are likewise:
they neither abide nor perish.
When a practitioner contemplates the mind and mental factors in this way, they do not apprehend any phenomena.
One should know that the phenomena which serve as objects of apprehension are ultimately empty and quiescent; therefore,
they are termed "pure."
Knowing that all phenomena are like illusions, lacking both self-nature and other-nature,
being fundamentally non-arisen and thus now non-extinguished—
what does such a statement mean?
The previously mentioned breaking of unarisen thoughts of desire through the application of right mindfulness by means of the twelve matters should be explained in detail for each individual case.
When the practitioner observes in this manner:
Furthermore, one should recognize that there are three kinds of mind:
first, the observation of the distracted mind;
second, the observation of the concentrated mind.
Third is observing the observing mind.
What is meant by "observing the distracted mind"?
It refers to [the mind] amidst the various matters previously described.
When a practitioner first begins their training and has not yet realized all phenomena,
disturbances arise throughout these objects of experience.
By contemplating with single-minded attention, they do not perceive the characteristics of the mind.
Thus, there is no distraction;
his mind is peaceful and secure whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.
His body and mind are tranquil, serene, and immovable.
This is the concentrated mind.
If one does not investigate this concentrated mind,
it will frequently give rise to defiled attachment.
As the Bodhisattva Vimalakīrti said:
"Attachment to the flavor of dhyāna is a bond for a bodhisattva.
Therefore, one should contemplate that the concentrated mind is unattainable."
Furthermore, there is no mind that can be said to abide anywhere;
one should know that this concentration arises from inversion.
When observing in this way, one perceives neither concentration nor non-concentration.
By not giving rise to greedy attachment, one attains liberation from the fetters of meditative concentration.
Thus, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* states:
"To arise through skillful means is the liberation of this bodhisattva."
This is called the contemplation of characteristics.
Having contemplated the concentrated mind with a concentrated mind,
the practitioner has not yet realized the principle.
Or one may reckon that "I am able to observe the mind," and for this reason does not perceive the marks of either concentration or distraction;
one should know that such wondrous wisdom is the most preeminent.
When one becomes attached to this wisdom of contemplation and immediately exalts oneself,
thinking that others cannot understand it—
such a state of mind is called an obstruction to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Being the same as those non-Buddhists, the *Śāstra* states:
"These non-Buddhists are attached to the wisdom that contemplates emptiness."
One cannot attain liberation.
Since the practitioner knows that the conceptualization of there being an "observer" constitutes a great obstacle to attaining Nirvana, [they must abandon it].
One should then turn back and contemplate the observing mind itself;
seeing no place of abiding and likewise no arising or ceasing,
one should know that ultimately there is no observer.
Furthermore, as for those who do not contemplate:
since there is no one who contemplates, who would contemplate all phenomena?
When one cannot apprehend the contemplating mind, one is immediately free from the conceptualization of contemplation.
Therefore, the *Śāstra* states:
"Conceptualization and mental observation have been eliminated;
the mind of frivolous proliferation has entirely ceased."
Immeasurable multitudes of sins are eliminated;
the pure mind is ever one-pointed.
Such a noble and wondrous person is then able to see Prajñā.
This is called contemplating the nature of the mind.
Therefore, the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra also says to contemplate the mind within the mind.
These are the three contemplations.
This refers to the three samādhis. Why is this so?
Because within the initial contemplation, one is able to shatter all various marks of existence (*nimitta*).
Not seeing either the internal or the external is the samādhi of emptiness.
In the second contemplation, one can destroy the very mark of emptiness.
This is called the samādhi of signlessness (animitta-samādhi).
In the third contemplation, one does not perceive an agent;
this is named the samādhi of wishlessness (apranihita-samādhi).
When a bodhisattva practices this samādhi,
they are able to destroy the three inversions, the three poisons, the characteristics of mind, consciousness, and mentation, as well as the flow of the three realms of existence;
they are also able to subdue the four kinds of māra-enemies.
Why is this so? For afflictions are entirely nothing but confusion and delusion.
Observing emptiness in this way,
one can understand that the nature of afflictions is without movement or change.
This is itself awakening.
Thus, the *Sarvadharmāpravṛttinirdeśa Sūtra* says:
"Lust is itself the path."
Hatred and delusion are also like this.
Within these three dharmas,
all Buddha-dharmas are fully contained.
If afflictions are awakening,
how could one further afflict awakening with awakening?
If one knows that the characteristic of afflictions is empty, that itself is awakening.
One transcends the demon of afflictions;
the same applies to the other three demons.
The reason for this is as follows:
As the *Suyāma-sūtra* says:
"The fool, regarding the aggregates, elements,
and sense bases, seeks to attain bodhi."
The aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are themselves [Bodhi];
apart from these, there is no Bodhi.
One should know that contemplating emptiness is precisely what delivers one from the Māra of the aggregates.
As the *Sāgaranāgarjuna-paripṛcchā-sūtra* (or *Siddhi-prārthanā-sūtra*) further states:
"Birth-and-death is nirvāṇa, because there is no falling away or arising.
One should know that contemplating emptiness is precisely the crossing over of the Māra of Death.
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra states:
"The suchness of the realm of Māra is itself the suchness of the realm of the Buddha;
the suchness of the realm of Māra is the suchness of the realm of the Buddha."
They are one and not two.
Because they are thus, one does not depart from the realm of Māra to attain the realm of the Buddha.
One should know that contemplating emptiness is precisely the means to transcend the Māra of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
When a bodhisattva practices the correct contemplation of the three emptinesses,
they immediately no longer fear the four māras; furthermore,
they do not perceive the four māras and are thus able to transcend them.
Therefore, the *Śāstra* states:
"With the exception of the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*),
everything else is termed the work of Māra."
If one can skillfully cultivate the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), there will be no demonic activities (*mārakarman*).
Therefore, the practitioner should skillfully contemplate this intent and practice samādhi;
ultimately, there will be no demonic activities.
If one departs from this contemplation and engages in conceptualization and recollection, one will certainly fall into the net of Māra.
Therefore, the Commentary states:
"If there is conceptualization and recollection, that is the net of Māra."
To be unmoving and non-discriminating is what is called the Seal of the Dharma (*dharmamudrā*).
Furthermore, when a practitioner is able to skillfully cultivate the three aforementioned contemplations,
they shatter all phenomena so that the mind has no attachment.
Although they know that sentient beings have the characteristic of emptiness, they constantly maintain great compassion and do not abandon any sentient being;
they study the various pāramitās and give rise to the ten powers.
Observing the various gateways of the dharma-realm, one nurtures all wholesome merits and virtues.
Chapter Six: Explaining the Signs of Realization of the Samādhi of Enlightenment-Mind. When the practitioner practices in this manner:
One will certainly enter the stage of the outer ordinary person (bāhyapṛthagjana).
Because of this stage, one is able to enter the first dwelling of the inner ordinary person (antarapṛthagjana), the Stage of Initial Resolve (prathamacittotpādavihāra).
What is meant by the "stage of the outer ordinary person"?
The external ordinary beings are the Iron Wheel Bodhisattvas;
they possess the nature of afflictions.
They are able to know the secret treasury of the Tathāgata;
they are also called the ten stages of faith of the external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*). What are their names?
First is the mind of faith;
second, the mind of mindfulness;
third, the mind of diligence.
Fourth, the mind of wisdom;
fifth, the mind of meditative concentration;
sixth, the non-regressive mind.
Seventh, the mind of dedication;
eighth, the protective mind;
ninth, the ethical mind.
Tenth, the mind of aspiration:
the practitioner skillfully cultivates three types of contemplation,
contemplating all phenomena.
When the mind abides in mindfulness as the breath ceases—
whether at the moment of entering meditative observation or while dwelling in dhyāna.
Or, while engaged in the four modes of deportment,
one may suddenly awaken to the fact that body and mind are suddenly spacious and open,
empty and still like a shadow, lacking any substantial reality.
When viewing all phenomena from without, they appear like floating clouds and are also like illusions and transformations;
one must certainly give rise to the wisdom of skillful means regarding them.
Furthermore, they know that all dharmas are neither born nor extinguished,
and that there is no duality between the limits of birth-and-death and nirvana.
If they hear the twelve divisions of the sutras, [they understand them as such].
Having also attained this wisdom through self-awakening and understanding,
one personally realizes the secret treasury within one's own body;
that the Three Jewels in their essential unity are no different from the Buddha.
They are also able to skillfully explain the essential points of the Dharma of the Three Vehicles with inexhaustible eloquence,
even though they have not yet realized the Truth.
Because one attains this realization through the power of a discerning wisdom that is clear and unimpeded,
it is called faith.
If such are the merits of the merit of the initial mind of faith, how much more so for the subsequent nine minds? Thus, one should speak of the causes and conditions of faith.
Therefore, it is known that the true mark of dharmas is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
It is the root of the myriad practices and the source of all spiritual beings.
Therefore, at all times, one should constantly contemplate non-arising and destroy various false views and deluded attachments.
One achieves right mindfulness and settles the mind in the principle of the single mark of suchness,
because there is nothing to be grasped or rejected.
The accomplishment of the mind of mindfulness consists in diligently practicing the three types of wisdom.
The mind of diligence consists in advancing toward enlightenment without indolence.
Because they diligently practice hearing, reflection, and cultivation with vigor,
they thereby obtain the eye of right wisdom and awaken to all phenomena.
That mind becomes increasingly luminous;
it is able to enter into the true nature of reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa) without attachment,
and is therefore called the "mind of wisdom" (prajñācitta).
By the power of wisdom, one destroys all delusions and distractions;
with the mind settled in its rational nature, one enters profound samādhi.
Therefore, it is called the "concentrated mind."
When the conditions of meditative concentration support and unite with right wisdom, one immediately attains firmness;
it is also able to nurture the great roots of goodness of compassion.
This is called the non-retrogressive mind.
With the courageous advancement of the mind-power, one is able to thoroughly comprehend all phenomena and enter entirely into non-arising.
At that time, whatever deeds are performed all tend toward bodhi.
To adorn the myriad practices is the mind of dedication that universally bestows upon all sentient beings;
it is the diligent mind that causes sublime goodness to blossom and nurtures its growth.
It is called "protecting the mind" because it prevents various faults from entering and damaging the roots of goodness; thus,
it is able to effectively ward off internal non-virtue.
One should also strictly guard against external evils.
To prevent such evils, one cultivates two kinds of precepts:
those concerning the gravity of intrinsic nature and those regarding the avoidance of subtle transgressions that provoke worldly reproach.
Therefore it is called the "mind of precepts.
Being able to internally prevent all outflows (āsrava) and externally adorning oneself with the precepts, it is so named.
At that time, the mind is free from obscuration;
the wisdom that cultivates principle becomes increasingly clear and manifest.
Having thus understood non-arising, [one realizes it].
When contemplating the principle,
one truly does not see any sentient beings to be delivered,
nor any afflictions to be severed.
The Dharma-gate can be entered;
the Buddha-way can be accomplished.
At that time, the Bodhisattva fears losing great compassion and falling into the stage of the two vehicles.
He then thought:
"In the emptiness of all phenomena,
there should be neither sentient beings nor the fruit of Buddhahood."
However, within the conventional truth, it is not that sentient beings, up to and including the Buddha-way, do not exist.
Yet, because all sentient beings do not know emptiness, they revolve through the five destinies; this is truly to be pitied.
I shall, for the sake of these deluded sentient beings,
give rise to great vows and increase my bodhicitta,
making this aspiration:
I vow that when I attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*),
I shall know that sentient beings are both empty and not empty;
even so shall it be with respect to bodhi and the Buddha-way.
Because they understand emptiness, they give rise to the great vow and bring it to fulfillment.
Abiding in this stage,
because they are able to know emptiness, they transcend the stage of ordinary beings.
Because one knows it is not empty, one transcends the stage of the śrāvakas.
To neither abide in emptiness nor abide in non-emptiness is called the Middle Way.
Practicing this Middle Way is the true and correct vow.
Therefore, it is called the "vow-mind.
When a bodhisattva abides in these ten minds, they are said to be in the stage of the iron wheel and are termed an "outer ordinary person" (bāhyapṛthagjana).
This person, though possessing afflictions, is able to know the secret treasury of the Tathāgata;
they attain wisdom resembling the Middle Way and abide in the dhyāna of intrinsic nature.
By skillfully cultivating these ten kinds of mind,
the mind becomes developed and enlightened; one realizes the Tathāgatagarbha,
awakens to all dharmas, and attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, one first attains entry into the Stage of Resolute Mind (*cittotpāda-vihāra*).
Abiding in this position, one enters the stage of the Inner Worldlings (*antarapṛthagjana*),
which is called the Copper Wheel Stage (*tāmracakra-vihāra*).
It is also called the perfection of the wisdom of hearing;
it is also called the nature of the stage of cultivation;
and it is also called the patience of subduing.
