It is also called the Ten Vows;
it is also called the Resolve for Enlightenment;
it is also called the Wisdom of the Path.
It is also called "the non-arising of arising," and it is also called "opening the Buddha's knowledge and vision.
There are immeasurable such alternative names.
Therefore, the reason it is initially called the "Stage of Generating the Resolve" (Cittotpāda-vihāra) is that from the very moment the practitioner first generates the resolve,
although they possess great loving-kindness and great compassion, [they have not yet fully realized them].
Although they possess immeasurable merit through meditative concentration and wisdom,
they have not yet attained the prajñā of the true mark;
thus, while they have indeed resolved their minds [on enlightenment], this is not yet called "abiding."
It is at this stage that one first accords with principle;
therefore, it receives the name "attainment" (*pratilambha*).
Thus, the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* says:
The wisdom that enters into principle is called "abiding.
Furthermore, another explanation states:
"The abiding of the arousal of the mind" (cittotpāda-vihāra).
"Arising" (udaya) means to unfold or manifest.
"Abiding" (sthiti) refers to attaining a state of stable rest.
This signifies the initial unfolding and realization of the principle of the Tathāgatagarbha.
One attains the state of peaceful abiding in non-arising.
Possessing these two meanings,
it is also called the Stage of Resolving the Mind (Cittotpāda-vihāra).
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva dwells in this stage,
they possess all meditative concentrations as well as difficult-to-attain concentrations. Why is this so?
There are three types of practitioners of dhyāna: first,
those who practice dhyāna for the sake of dwelling in the joy of the Dharma.
In the initial stage, one is able to sever all afflictions of the three realms,
exhausting them forever without remainder;
thus, one has no attachment or craving for any phenomena.
All meditative concentrations (dhyāna-samādhi) give rise to unconditioned mastery free from craving and views.
Second, regarding the practitioner who gives birth to samādhis:
upon entering the stage of the first abiding (prathamā bhūmi), they are able to produce immeasurable samādhis of the lineage of the ten powers (daśabala).
Third, regarding the dhyāna for benefiting sentient beings:
upon entering this stage, one may either behold the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time face-to-face,
or possess great dhāraṇī and unimpeded eloquence.
To benefit sentient beings,
they may attain the six supernormal powers and deliver others through the practice of sameness.
This is called the first stage, which is endowed with the three kinds of *sarvārtha-dhyāna*.
When one attains the *durlabha-dhyāna*,
there are likewise three kinds.
Upon entering this stage and casting off this body,
although one is free from the karmic bonds of birth and death,
one is nevertheless able to give rise to a body born of the dharma-nature.
Manifesting various bodies throughout the twenty-five realms of existence,
one enters these two stages; within them,
one will certainly transcend all dharma-gates realized by the three vehicles.
When entering this stage, all merits within every moment of thought are directed toward bodhi; thus,
the *Necklace Sūtra* (*Yingluo jing*) says:
The three types of worthy bodhisattvas naturally flow into the great ocean of wondrous enlightenment;
this is called the fulfillment of the three kinds of difficult dhyānas within the stage of the initial resolve.
The Bodhisattva is fully endowed with the dhyāna of intrinsic nature.
The dhyāna of all meanings is the true first stage.
The worthy person who has entered into principle is said to abide within the womb of the sages and to have attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Furthermore, they fully know the dharma-gates of the higher stages;
within a single moment of mind, they are complete in the ten thousand practices,
and their immeasurable merits are inexhaustible.
The remaining nine abodes and ten practices,
the ten vajra-stages, equal-enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment—
these are the realms of all Buddhas.
This is what is known by the Bodhisattva;
how could it be measured by the ordinary consciousness of common people?
This, then, is a brief explanation of the practice of the Samādhi of the Awakening Mind.
This is the initial stage. Within this,
the practitioner should properly grasp its meaning and practice it with diligence.
